{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}{{Short description|Indication of topological symmetry groups to topological condensed matter
}}The '''periodic table of topological insulators and topological superconductors''', also called '''tenfold classification of topological insulators and superconductors''', is an application of [[topology]] to [[condensed matter physics]]. It indicates the [[Group (mathematics)|mathematical group]] for the [[Topological property|topological invariant]] of the [[topological insulator]]s and [[topological superconductor]]s, given a dimension and discrete symmetry class.<ref name="Chiu 2016">{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1103/RevModPhys.88.035005 | last = Chiu| first = C. |author2=J. Teo|author3=A. Schnyder |author4=S. Ryu  | title = Classification of topological quantum matter with symmetries| journal = Rev. Mod. Phys.| volume = 88 | issue = 35005 | year = 2016 | article-number = 035005| arxiv = 1505.03535| bibcode = 2016RvMP...88c5005C| s2cid = 119294876}}</ref> The ten possible discrete symmetry families are classified according to three main symmetries: [[C-symmetry|particle-hole symmetry]], [[T-symmetry|time-reversal symmetry]] and [[Chirality (physics)|chiral symmetry]]. The table was developed between 2008–2010<ref name="Chiu 2016" /> by the collaboration of Andreas P. Schnyder, [[Shinsei Ryu]], Akira Furusaki and Andreas W. W. Ludwig;<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schnyder |first1=Andreas P. |last2=Ryu |first2=Shinsei |last3=Furusaki |first3=Akira |last4=Ludwig |first4=Andreas W. W. |date=2008-11-26 |title=Classification of topological insulators and superconductors in three spatial dimensions |url=https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.78.195125 |journal=Physical Review B |volume=78 |issue=19 |article-number=195125 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.78.195125|arxiv=0803.2786 |bibcode=2008PhRvB..78s5125S }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ryu |first1=Shinsei |last2=Schnyder |first2=Andreas P |last3=Furusaki |first3=Akira |last4=Ludwig |first4=Andreas W W |date=2010-06-17 |title=Topological insulators and superconductors: tenfold way and dimensional hierarchy |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1367-2630/12/6/065010 |journal=New Journal of Physics |volume=12 |issue=6 |article-number=065010 |doi=10.1088/1367-2630/12/6/065010 |issn=1367-2630|arxiv=0912.2157 |bibcode=2010NJPh...12f5010R }}</ref> and independently by [[Alexei Kitaev]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Kitaev |first=Alexei |title=AIP Conference Proceedings |date=2009 |chapter=Periodic table for topological insulators and superconductors |journal=Advances in Theoretical Physics: Landau Memorial Conference |volume=1134 |issue=1 |chapter-url=https://pubs.aip.org/aip/acp/article/1134/1/22-30/815164 |language=en |publisher=AIP |pages=22–30 |doi=10.1063/1.3149495|arxiv=0901.2686 |bibcode=2009AIPC.1134...22K }}</ref>

These table applies to topological insulators and topological superconductors with an energy gap, when particle-particle interactions are excluded. The table is no longer valid when interactions are included.<ref name="Chiu 2016" />

The topological insulators and superconductors are classified here in ten symmetry classes (A,AII,AI,BDI,D,DIII,AII,CII,C,CI) named after Altland–Zirnbauer classification, defined here by the properties of the system with respect to three operators: the time-reversal operator ''<math>T </math>'', charge conjugation <math>C</math> and chiral symmetry <math>S</math>. The symmetry classes are ordered according to the Bott clock (see below) so that the same values repeat in the diagonals.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Topology course team |date=2021 |title=10 symmetry classes and the periodic table of topological insulators |url=https://topocondmat.org/w8_general/classification.html |access-date=2024-09-13 |website=Online course on topology in condensed matter - TU Delft}}</ref>

An X in the table of "Symmetries" indicates that the symmetry of the [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] is broken with respect to the given operator. A value of ±1 indicates the value of the operator squared for that system.<ref name=":1" />

The dimension indicates the dimensionality of the systes: 1D (chain), 2D (plane) and 3D lattices. It can be extended up to any number of positive integer dimension. Below, there can be four possible group values that are tabulated for a given class and dimension:<ref name=":1" />

* A value of 0 indicates that there is no topological phase for that class and dimension.
* The group <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> indicates that the topological invariant can take integer values (e.g. ±0,±1,±2,...).
* The group of <math>2\mathbb{Z}</math> indicates that the topological invariant can take even values (e.g. ±0,±2,±4,...).
* The group of <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> indicates that the topological invariant can take two values (e.g ±1).

=== Physical examples ===
The non-chiral [[Su–Schrieffer–Heeger model]] (<math>d=1</math>), can be associated with symmetry class BDI  with an integer <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> topological invariant due to [[gauge invariance]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sachdev |first=Subir |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZVewEAAAQBAJ&dq=ssh+model+bdi+class&pg=PA258 |title=Quantum Phases of Matter |date=2023-04-13 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-009-21269-4 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Huber |first=Sebastian |url=https://cmt-qo.phys.ethz.ch/education/spring-semester-2013--topological-quantum-numbers-in-condensed-m.html |title=Topological quantum numbers in condensed matter systems |publisher=ETH Zurich |year=2013 |chapter=5 Topological insulators and superconductors}}</ref> The problem is similar to the [[Quantum Hall effect|integer quantum Hall effect]] and the [[quantum anomalous Hall effect]] (both in <math>d=2</math>) which are A class, with integer <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> [[Chern number]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Altland |first1=Alexander |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZdPQEAAAQBAJ&dq=quantum+hall+effect+%22class+A%22&pg=PA464 |title=Condensed Matter Field Theory |last2=Simons |first2=Ben |date=2023-09-14 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-49460-1 |language=en}}</ref>

Contrarily, the [[Kitaev chain]] (<math>d=1</math>) is also in BDI class, but in the presence of a magnetic field it becomes an example of symmetry class D, with a <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> binary topological invariant.<ref name=":2" /> Similarly, the <math>p_x+ip_y</math> superconductors (<math>d=2</math>) are also in class D, but with a <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> topological invariant.<ref name=":2" />

The [[quantum spin Hall effect]] (<math>d=2</math>) described by Kane–Mele model is an example of AII class, with a  <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> topological invariant.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Stanescu |first=Tudor D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EKYIEQAAQBAJ&dq=quantum+spin+hall+effect+%22class+AII%22&pg=PA182 |title=Introduction to Topological Quantum Matter & Quantum Computation |date=2024-07-02 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-040-04191-8 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Discrete symmetry classes ===
There are ten discrete symmetry classes of topological insulators and superconductors, corresponding to the ten Altland–Zirnbauer classes of [[random matrix|random matrices]]. They are defined by three symmetries of the Hamiltonian <math>\hat{H} = \sum_{i,j} H_{ij} c_i^{\dagger} c_j</math>, (where <math>c_i</math>, and <math>c_i^{\dagger}</math>, are the annihilation and creation operators of mode <math>i</math>, in some arbitrary spatial basis) : [[T-symmetry|time-reversal symmetry]], particle-hole (or [[C-symmetry|charge conjugation]]) symmetry, and [[Chirality (physics)|chiral]] (or sublattice) symmetry.

* Chiral symmetry is a unitary operator <math>S</math>, that acts on <math>c_i</math>, as a unitary rotation (<math>S c_i S^{-1} = (U_S)_{ij} c_j</math>,) and satisfies <math>S^2 = 1</math>. A Hamiltonian <math>H</math> possesses chiral symmetry when <math> S\hat{H}S^{-1}=-\hat{H}</math>, for some choice of <math>S</math> (on the level of first-quantised Hamiltonians, this means <math>U_S</math> and <math>H</math> are anticommuting matrices).

* Time-reversal symmetry (TRS) is an antiunitary operator <math>T</math>, that acts on <math>\alpha c_i</math>, (where <math>\alpha</math>, is an arbitrary complex coefficient, and <math>^*</math>, denotes [[Complex conjugate|complex conjugation]]) as <math>T \alpha c_i T^{-1} = \alpha^* {(U_T)}_{ij}c_j</math>. It can be written as <math>T = U_T \mathcal{K}</math> where <math>\mathcal{K}</math> is the complex conjugation operator and <math>U_T</math> is a [[unitary matrix]]. Either <math>T^2 = 1</math> or <math>T^2 = -1</math>. A Hamiltonian with time reversal symmetry satisfies <math>T\hat{H}T^{-1} = \hat{H}</math>, or on the level of first-quantised matrices, <math>U_T H^* U_T^{-1} = H</math>, for some choice of <math>U_T</math>.

* Charge conjugation or particle-hole symmetry (PHS) <math>C</math> is also an antiunitary operator which acts on <math>\alpha c_i</math> as <math>C \alpha c_i C^{-1}  = \alpha^* (U_C^{\dagger})_{ji}c_j</math>, and can be written as <math>C = U_C \mathcal{K}</math> where <math>U_C</math> is unitary. Again either <math>C^2 =1</math> or <math>C^2 = -1</math> depending on what <math>U_C</math> is. A Hamiltonian with particle hole symmetry satisfies <math>C\hat{H}C^{-1} = - \hat{H}</math>, or on the level of first-quantised Hamiltonian matrices, <math>U_C H^* U_C^{-1} = - H</math>, for some choice of <math>U_C</math>.

In the [[Bloch's theorem|Bloch Hamiltonian formalism]] for [[Crystal structure|crystal structures]], where the Hamiltonian <math>H(k)</math> acts on modes of crystal momentum <math>k</math>, the chiral symmetry, TRS, and PHS conditions become 
*<math>U_S H(k) U_S^{-1} = -H(k)</math> (chiral symmetry)

*<math>U_T H(k)^* U_T^{-1} = H(-k)</math> (time-reversal symmetry),

* <math>U_C H(k)^* U_C^{-1} = -H(-k)</math> (particle-hole symmetry).

It is evident that if two of these three symmetries are present, then the third is also present, due to the relation <math>S= TC</math>.

The aforementioned discrete symmetries label 10 distinct discrete symmetry classes, which coincide with the Altland–Zirnbauer classes of random matrices.

=== Equivalence classes of Hamiltonians ===
A bulk Hamiltonian in a particular symmetry group is restricted to be a [[Hermitian matrix]] with no zero-energy eigenvalues (i.e. so that the spectrum is "gapped" and the system is a bulk insulator) satisfying the symmetry constraints of the group. In the case of <math>d>0</math> dimensions, this Hamiltonian is a continuous  function <math>H(k)</math> of the <math>d</math> parameters in the Bloch momentum vector <math> \vec{k}</math> in the  [[Brillouin zone]]; then the symmetry constraints must hold for all <math>\vec{k}</math>.

Given two Hamiltonians <math>H_1</math> and <math>H_2</math>, it may be possible to continuously deform <math>H_1</math> into <math>H_2</math> while maintaining the symmetry constraint and gap (that is, there exists continuous function <math>H(t, \vec{k})</math> such that for all <math>0 \le t \le 1</math> the Hamiltonian has no zero eigenvalue and symmetry condition is maintained, and <math>H(0, \vec{k} ) = H_1( \vec{k})</math> and <math>H(1, \vec{k} ) = H_2( \vec{k})</math>). Then we say that <math>H_1</math> and <math>H_2</math> are equivalent.

However, it may also turn out that there is no such continuous deformation. in this case, physically if two materials with bulk Hamiltonians <math>H_1</math> and <math>H_2</math>, respectively, neighbor each other with an edge between them, when one continuously moves across the edge one must encounter a zero eigenvalue (as there is no continuous transformation that avoids this). This may manifest as a gapless zero energy edge mode or an electric current that only flows along the edge.

An interesting question is to ask, given a symmetry class and a dimension of the Brillouin zone, what are all the equivalence classes of Hamiltonians. Each [[equivalence class]] can be labeled by a topological invariant; two Hamiltonians whose topological invariant are different cannot be deformed into each other and belong to different equivalence classes.

For example, a (real symmetric) Hamiltonian in symmetry class AI can have its <math>n</math> positive eigenvalues deformed to +1 and its <math>N-n</math> negative eigenvalues deformed to -1; the resulting such matrices are described by the union of real [[Grassmannians]] <math>\bigcup_{n=0}^\infty \mathrm{Gr}(n, N) = \bigcup_{n=0}^\infty \mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm \mathrm O(n)\times \mathrm \mathrm O(N-n)</math>

There may also exist weak topological invariants (associated to the fact that the suspension of the Brillouin zone is in fact equivalent to a <math>d+1</math> sphere wedged with lower-dimensional spheres), which are not included in this table. Furthermore, the table assumes the limit of an infinite number of bands, i.e. involves <math>N \times N</math> Hamiltonians for <math>N \to \infty</math>.

The table also is [[Bott periodicity theorem|periodic]] in the sense that the group of invariants in <math>d</math> dimensions is the same as the group of invariants in <math>d+8</math> dimensions. In the case of no anti-unitary symmetries, the invariant groups are periodic in dimension by 2.

For nontrivial symmetry classes, the actual invariant can be defined by one of the following integrals over all or part of the Brillouin zone: the [[Berry connection and curvature|Chern number]], the [[Wess-Zumino]] [[winding number]], the [[Chern–Simons theory|Chern–Simons invariant]], the Fu–Kane invariant.

=== Dimensional reduction and Bott clock ===
The periodic table also displays a peculiar property: the invariant groups in <math>d</math> dimensions are identical to those in <math>d-1</math> dimensions but in a different symmetry class. Among the complex symmetry classes, the invariant group for A in <math>d</math> dimensions is the same as that for AIII in <math>d-1</math> dimensions, and vice versa. One can also imagine arranging each of the eight real symmetry classes on the Cartesian plane such that the <math>x</math> coordinate is <math>T^2</math> if time reversal symmetry is present and <math>0</math> if it is absent, and the <math>y</math> coordinate is <math>C^2</math> if particle hole symmetry is present and <math>0</math> if it is absent. Then the invariant group in <math>d</math> dimensions for a certain real symmetry class is the same as the invariant group in <math>d-1</math> dimensions for the symmetry class directly one space clockwise. This phenomenon was termed the Bott clock by [[Alexei Kitaev]], in reference to the [[Bott periodicity theorem]].<ref name="Chiu 2016" /><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://topocondmat.org/w8_general/classification.html|title=General approach to topological classification|last=Ryu|first=Shinsei|work=Topology in Condensed Matter|access-date=2018-04-30|language=en}}</ref>

The Bott clock can be understood by considering the problem of [[Clifford algebra]] extensions.<ref name="Chiu 2016" /> Near an interface between two inequivalent bulk materials, the Hamiltonian approaches a gap closing. To lowest order expansion in momentum slightly away from the gap closing, the Hamiltonian takes the form of a Dirac Hamiltonian <math>H_\text{Dirac}(\vec{k}) = \sum_{j=1}^d \Gamma_j v_j k_j + m\Gamma_0 </math>. Here, <math>\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2, \ldots, \Gamma_d</math> are a representation of the Clifford Algebra <math>\lbrace \Gamma_i , \Gamma_j \rbrace = 2\delta_{ij}</math>, while <math>m\Gamma_0</math> is an added "mass term" that and anticommutes with the rest of the Hamiltonian and vanishes at the interface (thus giving the interface a gapless edge mode at <math>k=0</math>). The <math>m\Gamma_0</math> term for the Hamiltonian on one side of the interface cannot be continuously deformed into the <math>m\Gamma_0</math> term for the Hamiltonian on the other side of the interface. Thus (letting <math>m</math> be an arbitrary positive scalar) the problem of classifying topological invariants reduces to the problem of classifying all possible inequivalent choices of <math>\Gamma_0</math> to extend the Clifford algebra to one higher dimension, while maintaining the symmetry constraints.
